FAST

AUSTIN, Texas, Oct 25 : George Russell was searching for answers after finishing eighth in a US Grand Prix won by Formula One champion-in-waiting Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli on Sunday. The Briton started in sixth place on the grid at Austin's Circuit of the Americas, collected a five-second penalty for an incident with McLaren's Oscar Piastri and said he had no explanation for his lack of pace other than "just not being quick enough." “I need to try and understand why it is. It’s strange when you’re so far off, so hopefully there’s some answers somewhere. But, anyway, I don’t have one,” he told Sky Sports television. The result left Antonelli on the brink of a coronation, the title surely his for the taking in Mexico next weekend with Russell still his closest rival but now 123 points behind and with a maximum 125 to be won.

“The pace wasn't good on the first stint," Russell told reporters. “But when I came out of the pits on the hard (tyres), I probably did six laps where I was lapping the same pace as Kimi. But then I caught up with Oscar and I just couldn't overtake.  "Six good laps, 50 bad laps. I want to understand why the pace was so bad on the first stint." Team boss Toto Wolff said Russell had just struggled. "George for all of us in the team is a champion and has won in every category and I think he merits to be put in the group of the very best ones. And we've seen that last year," said the Austrian. "This year ... we see this variability in results. When we land the car in a way that suits him, he's absolutely fast. But when it drops out of that operational window, he struggles. And he struggles more than maybe Kimi. "We just have to work it out with him, how there can be such a difference in driving, in performance. Because George is not half a second slower, three tenths slower than Kimi. That's just absolutely not the case."

Source: Reuters

SYDNEY, Oct 26 : Share markets got off to a cautious start on Monday as oil eased from six-month highs ahead of a week packed with central bank meetings and company earnings that will further test investor confidence in the AI boom. Brent oil slipped 1.0 per cent to $115.48 amid reports Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Sunday as part of an effort to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the United States. Brent futures jumped 6.2 per cent last week to their highest weekly close since mid-2022 as Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over energy supplies. US crude futures fell 1.1 per cent to $102.08 a barrel. Japan's Nikkei dipped 0.8 per cent, after losing 4.0 per cent last week, while South Korea fell 0.4 per cent, having shed almost 19 per cent so far this month. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.1 per cent.

The inflationary pulse from oil is likely to alarm all the central banks meeting this week, with hikes seen as just a matter of time even if some hold for now. "The main message from global central banks grappling with this year's macroeconomic surprises is that a relatively shallow rate hike cycle is underway," said Bruce Kasman, global head of economics at JPMorgan. "G3 central banks are likely to remain on hold, but Canada should start its tightening cycle and first moves are expected from the UK and Sweden next month." New Zealand's central bank is widely expected to raise rates on Wednesday. Markets assume the US Federal Reserve will stand pat, but imply an 80 per cent chance it will pull the trigger in December. Much the same is priced in for the Bank of Japan and the European Central Bank. A key reading on US core inflation should show cost pressures remained elevated at 3.1 per cent in September, while the economy is forecast to have grown at a brisk 3.2 per cent annualised pace thanks in part to furious spending on data centres. "The Fed is set to skip raising rates at its October meeting but is likely to deliver a second hike in December," analysts at Goldman Sachs said in a note. "The most important risk is that oil futures are above our forecasts, largely reflecting concerns about potential further conflict with Iran," they added. "The more extreme and long-lasting the energy shock becomes, the more Fed participants will worry that inflationary pressures could broaden." HYPERSCALERS TO TEST AI HYPE On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq futures both edged up 0.2 per cent. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures firmed 0.2 per cent, while DAX futures gained 0.1 per cent.  Earnings highlights will include the hyperscalers Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, among one-third of S&P 500 companies reporting. Results from Intel and Sandisk also could influence the AI trade. Consensus on Microsoft is for $90.6 billion of revenue and an adjusted EPS of $4.73, with Amazon at $202 billion of revenue and EPS around $1.97. Alphabet revenue is seen at $128 billion and EPS of $3.00. Equity valuations have been tested by higher bond yields, though Treasuries did manage a rally last week before running into renewed selling on Friday. Yields on 10-year Treasuries were at 5.0 per cent, but off a peak of 5.36 per cent hit early in the month. In currency markets, the Japanese yen retained its safe-haven appeal at 157.00 per dollar, having gained around 0.8 per cent last week. The euro held steady at $1.1204 as political unrest in France kept investors wary, though the country did escape a credit downgrade last week. Sterling held at $1.3346 with Britain's new finance minister, John Healey, set to deliver his first budget on Wednesday against a backdrop of rising global borrowing costs and high energy prices due to the Iran war. The Brazilian real was yet to trade in Asia as Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday, the country's electoral court said. In commodity markets, non-interest-bearing gold was a fraction firmer at $4,001 an ounce, having fallen more than 4 per cent last week. [GOL/]

Source: Reuters

item.description: A shock comeback returns Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva to power for a fourth term, bucking polls and slowing Latin America’s right-wing surge.

Lula, Brazil's iconic working class president, wins historic fourth term in dramatic comeback

A shock comeback returns Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva to power for a fourth term, bucking polls and slowing Latin America’s right-wing surge.

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking reelection, waves after voting in the presidential runoff in Sao Bernardo do Campo, Brazil, on Oct 25, 2026. (Photo: AP/Andre Penner)

FAST

SAO PAULO: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday (Oct 25), the country's electoral court said, in a shock result that defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century, defeated Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. The senator had finished first in the election's first round and hoped to revive his father's far-right movement. At times, Lula's reelection looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers' Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices, while sweeping societal changes left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers. Lula's victory marks another comeback in a career full of them. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.

"He is a statesman, a giant," leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters. UNLIKELY PATH TO VICTORY Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula's familiar embrace over Bolsonaro's novelty. "People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights," he said. During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term. He warned Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil's sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power. Lula's win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington's agenda on security and migration. Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist "would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance".

Supporters of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva cheer as presidential runoff results are announced in Sao Paulo, on Oct 25, 2026. (Photo: AP/Natacha Pisarenko)

COMEBACK KING Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil's return to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second in the first round. Lula, who was president between 2003 and 2011, campaigned on a potent mix of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians. These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public transport, which has to be formally submitted to Congress, to a 15 per cent increase in his trademark welfare program that is already being implemented. Lula also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil's biggest labour reform in decades, which passed with wide support in Congress. CHALLENGING LEGISLATIVE REALITY Still, Lula's fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s. Combined, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control over 280 seats in the lower house and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable majorities in both chambers.

Supporters of Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL) gather on a road after polls closed in the presidential runoff election, in Porto Alegre, Brazil, on Oct 25, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Diego Vara)

"He is likely to be a lame duck from the start," said Oliver Stuenkel, a professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation in São Paulo. The incoming legislature will likely deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress, Stuenkel said, predicting Lula will face waning influence over Supreme Court nominations, unwieldy party coalitions, and even the threat of impeachment. ECONOMIC HEADWINDS Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow a meagre 2.3 per cent next year, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82 per cent of GDP, the highest since the pandemic. The president's critics blame spending, though interest costs have driven most of the increase in debt. Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model. Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign. The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favour businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could fuel social upheaval.

FAST

AUSTIN, Texas, Oct 25 : Kimi Antonelli has given his Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff nine wins to get excited about this season but the Italian's dominant drive from pole position at Sunday's US Grand Prix took that to another level. The 20-year-old, set to become the youngest ever Formula One champion in Mexico next weekend, won by more than 13 seconds on a one-stop strategy. His teammate and closest title rival George Russell, now 123 points behind with 125 still to be won, started sixth and finished eighth - just enough to keep the championship hanging by a thread. "On Kimi's side the main headline is that for me (that's) the best race that he's delivered so far," Wolff said.

"Getting off the start with the inferior tyre and then controlling it (the race) at all times. The race of a champion who isn't the champion yet, but exceptional. "I think he's outperformed the car. His driving style just glues with the car." Wolff, reminded that Antonelli has had some special wins already this season including at his home Italian Grand Prix from the back of the grid as well as Monaco and Spa, accepted that sometimes he struggled to remember past races. "Both of them were pretty good," he said in reference to Monza. "But the headline, this is the best, we can keep." Antonelli was happy to agree with the boss. "I think it was one of the best, because of how we built up during the weekend," he told reporters. "And, you know, it was a great team effort as well today, especially with the strategy, believing in the one-stop. And, yeah, it was a really great team effort, and they all deserve this result today. "Monza, we clearly had the fastest car. We were just super quick, so of course it was incredibly special coming from the back," he added. "But it was also a track where it was relatively easy to overtake, and we were so quick. But definitely, Monza was a super special one, and one that I will remember forever. But, you know, this one probably, in terms of execution, was better ... the way we built the performance throughout the weekend was very good."

item.title: Serbia's Vucic concedes defeat in historic election win for student protest movement
item.description: Aleksandar Vucic has held power in Serbia since 2014, and his defeat heralds a new political era for the Balkan country.

Serbia's Vucic concedes defeat in historic election win for student protest movement

Aleksandar Vucic has held power in Serbia since 2014, and his defeat heralds a new political era for the Balkan country.

FAST

BELGRADE: Serbia's Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Sunday (Oct 25) that ends his long grip on power and heralds a new political era in the Balkan country. Vucic, a populist and nationalist, has dominated Serbian politics as prime minister or president since 2014. But he called snap elections in September after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024. "It is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won," Vucic said in a televised speech.

Within moments of his announcement, the streets of Belgrade erupted in celebration. Tens of thousands of people thronged along the city's main boulevards, with cars honking, people dancing and students shouting "victory" and "he's done". The students' win marks a profound political shift in the country of about 6 million people and is reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary's Viktor Orban in April. It may also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest, in some cases violently, against poor education standards and a lack of prospects. Vucic said the students would have between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament and that his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) would have 105, based on preliminary results. "Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard," said Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. "Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future." European leaders and officials congratulated the Student List on its victory, among them President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen and European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos. "We stand ready to ... work together to advance Serbia's future in the European Union," von der Leyen wrote on X. Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar assured the students of his country's support.

Supporters of the electoral list "Student List - Students Win" celebrate after Aleksandar Vucic, Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) prime ministerial candidate, conceded defeat in the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia, on Oct 25, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Marko Djurica)

RECORD TURNOUT SPURS STUDENTS TO VICTORY Lines snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country earlier in the day, and even Vucic waited for nearly two hours to vote in Belgrade. Pollsters and the election commission put turnout close to 70 per cent, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992. "(The turnout) did not surprise me because there was a large and strong mass that has formed throughout the past two years," said voter Katarina Petrovic. Vucic, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, was a strong incumbent and few in the student protest movement dared believe he would concede so fast. Supporters credit him with modernising Serbia's economy and building new highways, railways, schools and hospitals. "Some businessmen, some people will leave us but our structure is firm, we are very united, very strong, we are used to being in the opposition," Vucic said. UNCERTAINTY OVER THE STUDENTS' CANDIDATES Much remains unclear about how the student-backed candidates will fare. Their list of 250 largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, who was in tears after Vucic's announcement. However, it is unclear who will be prime minister and enact the students' domestic agenda, which aims to root out graft and improve schooling. Political analysts predict some kind of purge of Vucic allies in the police, security services and ministries. But the students have been quieter on their international ambitions. As Vucic did for years, they will have to juggle relations with China, a major investor, Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, and the European Union, Serbia's largest trading partner. "The biggest uncertainty is ... who is going to lead the government, who will be the key ministers, and how they will operate based on the promises they made to fight corruption, to reintroduce the rule of law, but also to re-establish Serbia's position in foreign policy," said Radivoje Grujic, a Warsaw-based election consultant. PROTEST MOVEMENT INCREASED PRESSURE The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster started small but quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression worsened in the period since. Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He has said the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss. Meanwhile, on the streets of Belgrade, a traditional brass band struck up, and a group including a man in a "students are champions" jumper floated balloons in the shape of the number 3, representing the number of the students' list of candidates. "We will drink a beer to celebrate, we will get drunk, we are so happy, I have no words to describe how much," said Andjela, a student who was with a group of friends. Dejan Soskic, a former central bank governor and a candidate of the Student List, called on people to maintain order and peace, and thanked voters for their civilised conduct during the electoral process.

Source: Reuters/dy

FAST

BARCELONA, Oct 25 : Real Madrid recorded just a second victory in eight games against Barcelona on Sunday night, with the return of Jose Mourinho to the fixture haunting the reigning champions. In the first Clasico of Mourinho's first spell at Real Madrid, Barcelona ripped his side to shreds in a 5-0 win at Camp Nou. A 2-1 win in the first Clasico of his second spell suggests Mourinho's Real Madrid can challenge Barcelona's recent LaLiga dominance in his first season back in Spain. Although the chances were shared out evenly, with Barcelona racking up more shots on goal, more possession and more passes throughout the match, those statistics were not an honest reflection of the game. Real Madrid played as if they had the answers to the test Barcelona posed. "The lads played an extraordinary match," said Mourinho in his press conference afterwards.

"Very organised, focused, and showing the courage to play the ball out from the back against an opponent that applied a lot of pressure." Time and again, Mourinho's side moved the ball with urgency and precision in their own half to escape Barcelona's pressing. Fede Valverde was praised for playing through injury by Mourinho, but above all he embodied the presence of mind to identify where the space was whenever the ball was turned over. The Uruguayan did so from the right-back position, despite stating in September 2025 that he was "not born to play as a full-back." Valverde later denied he had expressed any unwillingness to play in defence, but a number of Spanish outlets took this as a suggestion he was not pleased about doing so, and perhaps he was not on board with then-manager Xabi Alonso's style of management. For a third game in a row, the Real Madrid captain started at right-back and delivered a captain's performance. Valverde's impressive showing in his unfavoured position demonstrated Mourinho not only is finding tactical solutions to get the best out of his players, but is winning over the Real Madrid dressing room. Mourinho remarked that leaving Camp Nou just three points behind Barcelona "gives us peace of mind, and it's well deserved." The victory over Barcelona should help to boost morale and build unity within the Real Madrid squad. More importantly, Mourinho now has evidence his methods can help return Real Madrid to the summit of Spanish football.  "If we win today but lose at El Sardinero, it counts for nothing, because Madrid isn't playing to win at the Camp Nou," Mourinho said. "They’re playing to win the championship" — a statement that now looks closer to reality after two defeats in September had sown early doubts about Mourinho's plans.

US crude futures were down $1.60, or 1.55 per cent, at $101.67 per barrel by 0018 GMT. Brent crude futures were down $1.56 or 1.34 per cent at $115.16. BARCELONA, Oct 25 : Real Madrid became the first side to beat Barcelona in LaLiga this season, defeating the league leaders 2-1 at Camp Nou with a brace from Kylian Mbappe. Mbappe's 11th goal in 10 LaLiga matches secured victory for Jose Mourinho in his return to El Clasico 13 years after his first spell at Real Madrid ended. Real halved the gap to league leaders Barcelona to three points. Both sides created a series of half-chances early on, but Real's forays forward came with far more resolve. Barca manager Hansi Flick's frustration on the touchline served as evidence that Mourinho's game plan was functioning better than his own.

Barcelona had the chance to level before the break after a fortunate ricochet, but Lamine Yamal couldn't convert from close range. It was a set piece that undid Real in the 61st minute, with Pedri's reverse pass finding Raphinha in space in the box and the Brazilian finishing into the corner. Real's swift movement of the ball in their own half continued to expose the Barcelona backline in the early stages of the second half. However, following the goal, the visitors found it increasingly hard to escape Barcelona's pressing. Barcelona's attacks were now finishing with last-ditch blocks from the Real defence, even if Mourinho's side continued to carry a threat going forward. That defensive conviction was rewarded with three minutes remaining. A loose touch from Barcelona substitute Gabriel Jesus set Real on the counter-attack, and substitute Eduardo Camavinga had enough pace to get in behind the defence, before squaring the ball for Mbappe to tap into the empty net. Barcelona remain top of the standings with 27 points from 10 games, one ahead of Atletico Madrid in second place. Third-place Real Madrid are on 24 points. AUSTIN, Texas, Oct 25 : Kimi Antonelli delivered a dominant US Grand Prix victory for Mercedes on Sunday to stand on the brink of becoming Formula One's youngest ever champion with four rounds to spare in Mexico next weekend. The 20-year-old Italian did all he could to put the championship out of reach of his rivals in Texas but Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Mercedes teammate George Russell did just enough to delay the inevitable with fourth and eighth respectively.. Antonelli now needs to score only two points - a ninth place - in Mexico City to be sure of the title even if Russell wins. "It was the result we needed and the whole team deserve it so much," he said of his first win since Spain last month. "I know we're very close. We try to finish on a high and hopefully we can clinch it very soon".

LECLERC SECOND AND VERSTAPPEN THIRD  Ferrari's Charles Leclerc finished second, 13.078 seconds behind, in Sunday's race at Austin's Circuit of the Americas with Red Bull's Max Verstappen third and helped by a late virtual safety car that slowed a chasing Hamilton who finished one second down the road.            The win from pole position on a one-stop strategy was Antonelli's ninth in of the season and he now leads Russell by 123 points, and Hamilton by 124 with a maximum 125 remaining to be won and that reducing to 100 after Mexico. "The main headline is that for me (it is) the best race he's delivered so far," said Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff.  "The race of a champion who isn't the champion yet, but exceptional".    McLaren's reigning champion Lando Norris finished fifth on a one stop strategy after being passed by both Verstappen and Leclerc on lap 47 of 56 with his tyres struggling. Red Bull's Isack Hadjar was sixth, and ahead of McLaren's Oscar Piastri. Liam Lawson was ninth for Racing Bulls and Pierre Gasly took the final point for Alpine. Antonelli made a flying getaway and was 2.3 seconds clear at the end of the opening lap while the Ferrari pair took the fight to slow-starting Verstappen for second place. Leclerc went ahead, before being passed again by the Red Bull, and nearly made contact with Hamilton after the uphill scramble off the grid. The virtual safety car was briefly deployed on lap two to allow marshals to clear debris and Russell, who had started sixth, had to serve a five second penalty at his sole stop after stewards ruled he had gained an advantage on Piastri on the opening lap at Turn 13. Russell was then unable to find a way past the McLaren. "Six good laps, 50 bad laps," he said of his race. "I want to understand why the pace was so bad on the first stint. The penalty was a bit ridiculous as well, but that's the least of my worries after such a bad weekend. "For me, as long as we're in the constructors' (lead), that's the main thing. Obviously I'd like to finish best of the rest, but P2, P3, P5 is not champion, so it doesn't mean anything." Haas's Ollie Bearman also collected a 10 second penalty for causing a collision with Gasly and retired at the half-distance.

BRASILIA: Brazil's Supreme Court extended voting in the country's presidential election by two hours on Sunday (Oct 25), leading the electoral authority to pause a vote count that had already started publishing early-stage results. The election pits leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. Polls were initially set to close at 5pm Brasilia time (4am Monday, Singapore time) and will now close at 7pm after Supreme Justice Cristiano Zanin accepted a request by Lula's campaign to extend voting, pointing to public transportation issues in three cities in the state of Bahia. Zanin's decision landed right around the 5pm cutoff, when the electoral court had already started publishing results that showed Lula leading Bolsonaro with 0.25 per cent of ballot counted. Lula had 57.66 per cent of votes, compared with 42.34 per cent for Bolsonaro, the early count showed.

KYIV: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said US warnings about imminent Russian ballistic missile strikes , critical to Ukraine's air defences, had been fully restored after recent issues. "The issue of territories is a red line that can be discussed exclusively at the level of leaders," Zelenskyy said.

JERUSALEM: Billionaire American investor Bill Ackman on Sunday (Oct 25) said that Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich should not serve in Israel's next government, saying the two far-right politicians had caused enormous damage to the country's reputation. The public intervention by the prominent hedge fund manager, who is Jewish, comes just two days before Israel's general election, in which polls show a tight race between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition and the opposition. Ackman wrote on X that from the perspective of someone who had an understanding of how Israel was perceived in the United States, "Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have caused Israel enormous reputational damage with their statements and actions." "This will allow Israel to rebuild lost credibility, increase the opportunity for an expansion of the Abraham Accords, and enjoy a better relationship with Democrats and Republicans and Americans at large," he said. The Abraham Accords are the 2020 agreement, mediated by President Donald Trump's first administration, that saw Israel establish relations with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. It later reestablished official ties with Morocco. Representatives for Ben-Gvir and Smotrich did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

As ministers in Netanyahu's religious-nationalist coalition, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have overseen policies widely perceived as discriminatory against Israel's minority Arab population and Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank. Several countries, including Britain, Canada and Australia, have imposed sanctions on the two ministers over accusations that they have incited violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party is projected to win around 10 parliamentary seats at Tuesday's election, up from 6, while Smotrich's Religious Zionism is projected to win 8, up from 7. Ackman, who was visiting Israel last week, and who along with his wife Neri Oxman owns 5 percent of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, supported Donald Trump's candidacy for president in 2024. Trump last week publicly endorsed Netanyahu for prime minister. Nimrod Goren, the president of Israeli think tank Mitvim, said Ackman's statement appeared to reflect a desire among Trump's circles for Netanyahu to drop his far-right allies after the vote to form a 'unity government' with opposition parties. However, Gadi Eisenkot, the leading challenger to Netanyahu, and other opposition party leaders have ruled out forming a government with Israel's longest-serving prime minister. Speaking at a Tel Aviv conference on Thursday, Ackman praised Netanyahu, who he said had done a good job in protecting and defending Israel since the Oct 7 2023 Hamas attack. Thousands of Israelis rallied in Tel Aviv on Saturday calling for an independent inquiry into the attack that killed around 1,200 people.
